lines.text: A land conquered by Rome, defended by warrior princes, united as a kingdom and freed from a dictator. This is the story of Romania.
North of the Danube lay the kingdom of the Dacians, until the Roman emperor Trajan conquered it in 106. Its people came to speak a Latin tongue.
By the late thirteenth century, a castle stood at Bran in Transylvania, the fortress now often called Dracula's castle.
In the early 1300s, the principality of Wallachia took shape between the Carpathian mountains and the Danube.
Its people and their neighbours spoke the language of Romania, a Latin tongue in eastern Europe that would one day give its name to a nation.
East of the Carpathians, a second principality, Moldavia, rose soon after. Together the two lands would form Romania.
In Wallachia, Prince Vlad the Impaler fought the Ottomans and terrified his enemies. His name would inspire the legend of Dracula.
In Moldavia, Stephen the Great fought off the Ottomans too, and built painted monasteries that still stand.
In 1459, Bucharest first appears in the records. It would become the capital, once called the little Paris of the east.
In 1600, Michael the Brave briefly united Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia under one rule, a dream that would return.
In 1859, Wallachia and Moldavia chose the same prince, and the union that began modern Romania was made.
In the 1870s, work began on Peles Castle in the Carpathians, a fairy-tale home for King Carol the first.
Constantin Brancusi, born in a village in 1876, would carve sculptures of pure, simple forms such as Bird in Space.
In 1881, Romania, independent since 1878, became a kingdom.
That same year George Enescu was born, the composer and violinist who became the greatest figure of Romanian music.
And in 1918 came the birth of Nicolae Ceausescu, who would one day rule the country with an iron hand.
On the first of December 1918, Transylvania joined Romania. That day is now the national holiday.
Under communism, a girl named Nadia Comaneci was born. At fourteen she scored the first perfect ten in Olympic gymnastics.
Nicusor Dan, a mathematician born in 1969, would one day become mayor of Bucharest and then president.
In 1985, Ceausescu's vast palace rose in Bucharest, on land cleared of old neighbourhoods, one of the largest buildings in the world.
In December 1989, Romanians rose up. The uprising was violent, and it ended communist rule and Ceausescu's life.
In 2015, a fire at the Colectiv nightclub in Bucharest killed sixty-four people, and public anger brought down the government.
And in 2025, after the previous vote was annulled, a rerun election made Nicusor Dan president.
From Trajan's conquest to a free vote in Bucharest, Romania's long story carries on in Europe.
